writing.explanation:
A channel moves ownership between threads, so there is nothing left to lock and the flow of data is visible in the code. A mutex keeps one copy that several threads access in turn, which fits when the state is genuinely shared and each update must see it whole. It also serializes readers, so read-mostly state may suit an `RwLock` or a swapped `Arc` better. Choosing by shape rather than by habit is the answer being looked for.

A channel and a mutex organize ownership in different ways. With a channel, producers send owned messages to a receiver that handles them. This works well when one task can own the state and commands describe the changes. A mutex lets multiple tasks access one shared object, with exclusive access while a guard is held. This works well when callers need immediate coordinated reads or updates to a shared invariant. Neither is universally faster or simpler; the workload and failure path decide.

Consider an order book. A single owner task receiving add and cancel commands can serialize updates without exposing internal mutable state. If many workers only read an immutable configuration and rarely replace it, a read-oriented sharing strategy may be clearer than funneling every read through messages. A mutex around a small counter is straightforward, though an atomic may fit that narrow operation. Name the invariant before choosing the primitive.

Mention backpressure and shutdown in an interview answer. An unbounded channel can grow without limit if producers outpace the receiver. A bounded channel makes senders wait or fail when capacity fills. A receiving loop ends only after all sender handles are gone; an accidentally retained clone can keep it waiting. A mutex guard should not be held while doing slow I/O or calling unknown code. Show the interviewer how each design makes a particular failure visible, then explain the tradeoff in latency, ordering, and complexity.

When a result is required from the owner task, include a reply channel or request identifier. That extra protocol cost can make a simple mutex more attractive for a tiny local operation. Conversely, a channel may make shutdown and audit logging cleaner because all state changes pass through one place.

Interview follow-up: Explain why per-producer order does not necessarily define a meaningful global order for simultaneous requests.
writing.feedback: A channel models transfer, but does not eliminate capacity, shutdown or ordering design. A shared-state API can also be appropriate for a different access pattern.

recall.question: A consumer runs `for msg in rx { ... }`. All producer threads have finished, but the loop never ends. What is the likely cause?
recall.answer: The receiving loop ends only after every `Sender` handle is dropped. An accidentally retained clone, often the original `tx` kept in the spawning thread, keeps the channel open, so `recv` waits forever; `drop(tx)` lets it return an error and end the loop.

recall.question: When does a single owner task receiving commands over a channel suit shared state better than a mutex, and when does the mutex win?
recall.answer: An owner task fits when changes can be expressed as commands, such as add and cancel on an order book: updates are serialised in one place, which helps shutdown and audit logging. For a tiny local operation that needs an immediate result, the reply-channel protocol costs more than a short mutex section.
